::: {.why}
Every pricing method in week 39 is a simulation, so knowing the error of your integrator, and that it has two different rates depending on what you are measuring, prevents a class of silent inaccuracy.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Implement the Euler-Maruyama scheme and measure its strong and weak convergence rates against the exact solution.
- Say which rate matters for pricing an option and which matters for hedging a path.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Implement the scheme in qlib/derivatives/sde.py and measure both errors against the exact geometric Brownian motion solution: strong error as the mean absolute path difference, and weak error as the difference in the mean of a function of the terminal value. Plot both against the step size on log axes and read off the two slopes.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [15 min]{.task-min} Say which one you need: pricing depends on the distribution of the terminal value, so weak convergence is what matters and it is the faster of the two rates. Path-dependent hedging depends on the path, so strong convergence matters there and it is slower. Getting this wrong makes people use far smaller steps than they need for a European price.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Implement the exact simulation for geometric Brownian motion too, since it exists, and note that using the exact scheme where one is available removes the question entirely.
:::
:::
